# Introduction to the Business Problem

A store sells fruit, meat, fish, sweets and gold products. Customers buy
in person, on the store's website and through its catalog.

**The problem.** The store's marketing team has the budget for two
campaigns next quarter. It wants to aim each campaign at a different
group of customers, with its own offer and its own channel: the store,
the website or the catalog. If you had to split these customers into
two groups for those two campaigns, how would you do it, and how would
you explain the groups to the marketing team?

The dataset has one observation per customer, 2,240 customers. For each
customer we have an ID, the year of birth, annual household income, the
number of children and of teenagers at home, the days since the last
purchase, four counts of purchases (with a discount, on the website,
from the catalog and in the store), the visits to the website in a
month, and the amounts spent on fruit, meat, fish, sweets and gold
products over the last two years. The file also has education, marital
status, a date, and flags for marketing campaigns and complaints. We do
not use them. Wine spending is not in this file.

**Why clustering?** The store wants groups of customers who look alike
on income, children and how they buy. With 15 variables at once, nobody
can sort the customers by hand, and many of the variables move together.
K-means does the sorting from the distances between customers. Each
group it finds is a segment.

The question for this lab: can these 15 variables split the customers
into two segments that the store can name and act on? Which variables
separate the two segments? Does a second method find the same two groups?
What can this file not tell the store?

In this lab we use two groups. Section 4 shows two checks for the number
of groups. With real data we do not know the true number of groups, so
the checks help us choose a number and cannot prove it.

Keep the case PDF and the codebook open while you run code.

**Before you run anything.** Suppose you may use only income and the
number of children at home to split the customers into two groups. What
would you name the two groups? Name one kind of customer this split would
put in the wrong group, and say why. Talk this through with the person
next to you. We come back to it in section 7.

# Roadmap

1. **Load, summarize and look at correlations.** Find the missing
   incomes, check that wine spending is not in the file, drop the
   customers the lab does not use, keep the 15 variables, compare their
   standard deviations (SDs), and see which variables move together.
2. **Standardize the variables.** Why clustering needs z-scores, and what
   k-means does on the variables in their original units.
3. **Run k-means with two groups and read its output.** The parts of the
   `kmeans()` result one by one: `$cluster`, `$size`, `$centers`,
   `$withinss`, `$tot.withinss`, `$totss` and `$betweenss`.
4. **How many groups?** The elbow (1 to 8 groups) and the silhouette
   (2 to 8 groups) with `fviz_nbclust()`, then the silhouette of each
   customer with `fviz_silhouette()`. The lab keeps two.
5. **Profile and name the segments.** The group means in the original
   units, the two centers as a chart, and the two segments on income and
   meat spending with `fviz_cluster()`. Name each segment and choose the
   offer and the channel for its campaign.
6. **A second method: hierarchical clustering.** Ward linkage, cut
   into two groups, compared with k-means, and plotted as a dendrogram
   with `fviz_dend()`.
7. **What can the grouping not tell the store?** Write down one limit,
   then go back to the split from the start.

We stop there in class. Section 8 has six more questions to work on after
class.

# 1. Load, summarize and look at correlations

```{r}
#| label: setup
# This lab uses four packages. If you have not installed them, run this
# line once in the console, not in the notebook:
# install.packages(c("cluster", "factoextra", "dendextend", "ggplot2"))
library(cluster)     # silhouette()
library(factoextra)  # fviz_nbclust(), fviz_silhouette(), fviz_cluster(), fviz_dend()
library(dendextend)  # fviz_dend() uses it; its startup messages are expected
library(ggplot2)     # the plots
options(scipen = 999)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
cust <- read.csv("data/customer_personality.csv")
# dim() prints the number of customers and the number of variables.
dim(cust)
# colSums(is.na()) counts the missing values in each variable. We print
# only the variables with at least one.
na_count <- colSums(is.na(cust))
na_count[na_count > 0]
# str() shows each variable and its type.
str(cust)
# Is wine spending in the file? The spending variables all start with Mnt.
"MntWines" %in% names(cust)
grep("^Mnt", names(cust), value = TRUE)

# Question: How many customers are there, and how many variables? How
# many values are missing, and in which variable? Is wine spending in the
# file?
```

```{r}
#| label: row-rule
# Why? K-means needs a value for every variable, so a customer with no
# income cannot be clustered. Look also at the three highest incomes and
# the five earliest years of birth.
head(sort(cust$Income, decreasing = TRUE), 3)
head(sort(cust$Year_Birth), 5)

# The rule for this lab: drop the customers with no income and the one
# income of 666,666. The three earliest years of birth (1893, 1899 and
# 1900) stay in. After-class question 3 drops them and reruns k-means.
keep <- !is.na(cust$Income) & cust$Income != 666666
cust2 <- cust[keep, ]
nrow(cust2)
sum(!keep)

# Question: How many customers remain? How far is 666,666 from the second
# highest income? Would you believe a customer born in 1893?
```

```{r}
#| label: fifteen-variables
# Why? Clustering uses distances, and a distance needs numbers. ID is a
# label: rownames() attaches it to X, so the tables below show it.
# Education, marital status, the date, the campaign and complaint flags,
# Z_CostContact, Z_Revenue and Response stay out of the clustering.
vars <- c("Year_Birth", "Income", "Kidhome", "Teenhome", "Recency",
          "NumDealsPurchases", "NumWebPurchases", "NumCatalogPurchases",
          "NumStorePurchases", "NumWebVisitsMonth", "MntFruits",
          "MntMeatProducts", "MntFishProducts", "MntSweetProducts",
          "MntGoldProds")
X <- cust2[, vars]
rownames(X) <- cust2$ID
dim(X)
sum(is.na(X))

# summary() gives the smallest value, the quartiles, the mean and the
# largest value of each variable. head() shows the first customers: each
# observation is one customer's profile.
summary(X)
head(X)

# The SD of each variable, from smallest to largest, and the ratio of the
# largest SD to the smallest.
var_sd <- sapply(X, sd)
round(sort(var_sd), 2)
max(var_sd) / min(var_sd)

# Question: Which variable has the largest SD, and in what unit? Which has
# the smallest, and in what unit? If we measured the distance between two
# customers with these numbers as they are, which variable would decide
# who is close to whom?
```

```{r}
#| label: correlations
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.5
# Why? When two variables move together, the distance between two
# customers counts the same difference twice. cor() gives the correlation r
# of every pair of variables, from -1 to 1.
# Student Note: as a rule of thumb, |r| above 0.5 is a strong relationship.
R <- cor(X)
# The five pairs with the strongest correlation, positive or negative.
idx <- which(upper.tri(R), arr.ind = TRUE)
cor_pairs <- data.frame(var1 = rownames(R)[idx[, 1]], var2 = colnames(R)[idx[, 2]],
                        r = round(R[idx], 2))
head(cor_pairs[order(-abs(cor_pairs$r)), ], 5)
# The whole matrix as a heatmap: blue is positive, red is negative, and a
# darker cell is a stronger correlation.
cor_long <- data.frame(var1 = factor(rep(vars, times = length(vars)), levels = vars),
                       var2 = factor(rep(vars, each = length(vars)), levels = rev(vars)),
                       r = as.vector(R))
ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#C41230", mid = "white", high = "#1F5FA8",
                       limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r",
       title = "Correlations between the 15 variables") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

# Question: Which variables move together? Which variables move against
# income and the spending variables?
#
# Business Insight: When several variables rise together, a split of the
# customers will likely run along all of them at once. Keep the variables
# you found in mind when you read the centers in section 3.
```

# 2. Standardize the variables

**Why?** K-means measures how far apart two customers are and adds up the
differences on all 15 variables. In the original units, one dollar of
income counts as much as one child at home, and incomes run into the tens
of thousands, so income alone would decide who is close to whom.

**Formula.** For each variable, z = (x − mean) / SD.

**Intuition.** A z-score says how many SDs a customer is above or below
the mean of all customers. After standardizing, "high income" and "many
children" are on the same scale, and each variable has mean 0 and SD 1.

```{r}
#| label: z-scores
# scale() turns every variable into z-scores.
Xs <- scale(X)
# Check: every mean is 0 and every SD is 1.
round(colMeans(Xs), 2)
round(apply(Xs, 2, sd), 2)
# Income and meat spending for the first three customers, in their own
# units and in SDs.
X[1:3, c("Income", "MntMeatProducts")]
round(Xs[1:3, c("Income", "MntMeatProducts")], 2)

# Question: The first customer's income and meat spending are both above
# the average. Which of the two is further above it, counted in SDs?
#
# Student Note: Standardizing is a data preparation step, as in the
# principal component analysis (PCA) lab. Methods that use distances need
# it when the variables are in different units.
```

```{r}
#| label: units-vs-sds
# Why? K-means puts each customer with the nearest center, so the units
# decide what "near" means. Two groups, once on the variables in their
# original units and once in SDs. set.seed(467) and nstart = 20, as in the
# clustering slides.
set.seed(467)
km_raw <- kmeans(X, centers = 2, nstart = 20)
set.seed(467)
km_z <- kmeans(Xs, centers = 2, nstart = 20)
# The lowest and the highest income in each group of the run in the
# original units.
tapply(X$Income, km_raw$cluster, range)
# How many customers the two runs put together: the run in the original
# units down the side, the run in SDs across the top. The group numbers of
# the two runs are not matched, so the customers who change group are the
# two smaller counts.
table(original_units = km_raw$cluster, sds = km_z$cluster)

# Question: Do the income ranges of the two groups in the original units
# overlap? Which variable decided those groups?
#
# Discuss: On the Starbucks menu, without SDs the groups were calorie
# bands. Is it the same here? How many customers would change group if we
# moved to SDs? From now on we cluster in SDs.
```

# 3. Run k-means and read its output

**Why k-means?** It is fast on thousands of customers, and each group is
described by its center (also known as the centroid), the mean of
its customers, which is easy to explain to a marketing team.

**Intuition.** K-means starts from k centers chosen at random, where k is
the number of groups (here 2). It puts each customer with the nearest
center, moves each center to the mean of its customers, and repeats until
no customer changes group.

```{r}
#| label: kmeans-k2
# Why? One random start can stop at a worse grouping. nstart = 20 runs 20
# random starts and keeps the one with the smallest total within-group sum
# of squares. set.seed(467) makes the random starts the same on every
# computer.
set.seed(467)
km <- kmeans(Xs, centers = 2, nstart = 20)
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-labels
# Why? R numbers the groups 1 and 2 in the order it happens to find them.
# The numbers are labels only, and another computer can swap them. So that
# everyone in the room reads the same output, group 1 is the group with
# the lower mean income. If R found them the other way around, we swap the
# labels in every part of km. Swapping the labels moves no customer to
# another group.
if (km$centers[1, "Income"] > km$centers[2, "Income"]) {
  km$cluster <- 3L - km$cluster
  km$centers <- km$centers[2:1, ]
  rownames(km$centers) <- 1:2
  km$size <- km$size[2:1]
  km$withinss <- km$withinss[2:1]
}
group <- km$cluster
table(group)
```

```{r}
#| label: kmeans-groups
# kmeans() returns a list. These are the parts that describe the groups.
#
# $cluster: the group of each customer, 1 or 2, in the order of the observations.
# The names are the customer IDs. These are the segment labels.
head(km$cluster, 10)
# $size: the number of customers in each group.
km$size
# $centers: the mean of each variable in each group, in SDs. One line per
# group, one number per variable.
round(km$centers, 2)

# Question: How many customers are in each group? On which variables are
# the two centers farthest apart? On which are they almost the same?
#
# Interpret: A center of 1 on Income would mean that the group's mean
# income is one SD above the mean of all customers. We go back to the
# original units in section 5.
#
# Business Insight: A segment is only useful if it is large enough to be
# worth its own campaign. Is either group too small for that?
```

```{r}
#| label: kmeans-sums
# These parts say how tight the groups are.
#
# $withinss: for each group, the squared distance of each customer to the
# group's center, added up. Divided by the size, it is the spread per
# customer, which does not grow with the size of the group.
round(km$withinss, 1)
round(km$withinss / km$size, 2)
# $tot.withinss: the two added together. This is the number k-means makes
# as small as it can.
km$tot.withinss
# $totss: the same sum around the mean of all customers, before any
# grouping. In SDs it is (number of customers - 1) times 15.
km$totss
# $betweenss: totss minus tot.withinss, the part of the spread that lies
# between the groups. Its share of totss says how much of the spread the
# two groups explain.
km$betweenss
km$betweenss / km$totss

# Question: Which group is tighter, per customer? What share of the spread
# lies between the two groups?
#
# Student Note: A higher share is not always better. With one group per
# customer the share would be 1, and the store would learn nothing.
```

# 4. How many groups?

There is no outcome to check the groups against, so we use two checks.
`fviz_nbclust()` runs `kmeans()` for each number of groups, k, with the
`nstart` we give it, and plots the result.

```{r}
#| label: elbow
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
# Why? The elbow: the total within-group sum of squares for each k. It
# always falls as k grows, so we look for the k after which it falls much
# less: the bend in the curve. At k = 1 the total is totss.
# This chunk and the next take a few seconds each.
set.seed(467)
elbow_plot <- fviz_nbclust(Xs, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 8, nstart = 20)
elbow_plot + labs(title = "Elbow method", x = "Number of groups, k",
                  y = "Total within-group sum of squares")
# The numbers behind the plot, and how much the total falls from one k to
# the next.
wss <- setNames(elbow_plot$data$y, elbow_plot$data$clusters)
round(wss, 1)
round(-diff(wss), 1)

# Question: Where does the curve bend? How does the fall from 2 to 3
# groups compare with the fall from 1 to 2?
```

```{r}
#| label: silhouette
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
# Why? The silhouette of a customer compares a, its average distance to
# the customers of its own group, with b, its average distance to the
# customers of the nearest other group:
#   s = (b - a) / max(a, b), from -1 to 1.
# Near 1, the customer sits well inside its group. Near 0, it sits on the
# edge between two groups. Below 0, it is closer to the other group. The
# plot shows the mean over all customers for each k; the dashed line
# marks the highest.
# Student Note: as a rough guide, a mean above 0.5 means reasonable
# structure, a mean between 0.25 and 0.5 means weak structure that could
# be an accident of the method, and a mean below 0.25 means little or no
# structure.
set.seed(467)
sil_plot <- fviz_nbclust(Xs, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 8, nstart = 20)
sil_plot + labs(title = "Silhouette method", x = "Number of groups, k",
                y = "Mean silhouette width")
# The numbers behind the plot, for k = 2 to 8 (a silhouette needs at
# least two groups).
sil <- setNames(sil_plot$data$y, sil_plot$data$clusters)
round(sil, 3)

# Question: At which k is the mean silhouette highest? Do the elbow and
# the silhouette point to the same k? Where do these values fall on the
# rough guide?
#
# Discuss: The two checks need not agree, and with real data we do not
# know the true number of groups. Besides these two plots, what should
# decide how many segments the store works with? The lab uses k = 2.
```

```{r}
#| label: silhouette-k2
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
# Why? The mean hides how well each customer sits in its group.
# fviz_silhouette() plots one bar per customer, sorted within each group,
# and prints the mean of each group. The dashed line is the mean over all
# customers.
# dist() computes the distance between every two customers once.
# silhouette() needs it, and so does hierarchical clustering in section 6.
d <- dist(Xs)
sil2 <- silhouette(group, d)
fviz_silhouette(sil2, palette = c("#1F5FA8", "#C41230"))
# The number of customers with a negative silhouette, in each group.
table(group = group, negative = sil2[, "sil_width"] < 0)

# Question: Which group is tighter? In which group are the customers with
# a negative silhouette?
#
# Business Insight: Customers with a negative silhouette are closer to the
# other segment than to their own. An offer designed for their segment may
# not suit them.
```

# 5. Profile and name the segments

**Why?** K-means gives the group means, and we choose the names. A
segment becomes useful to the marketing team when it has a name that
matches its means in the original units and an offer and a channel for
its campaign.

```{r}
#| label: group-means
# The group means in the original units: group 1, group 2 and, last, all
# customers.
profile <- cbind(sapply(split(X, group), colMeans), all = colMeans(X))
round(profile, 1)
# The share of customers in each group with at least one child or
# teenager at home.
round(tapply(X$Kidhome + X$Teenhome > 0, group, mean), 2)
# The share with at least one small child at home (Kidhome above 0).
round(tapply(X$Kidhome > 0, group, mean), 2)

# Which variables separate the two groups? For each variable, the share of
# its spread (its sum of squares) that lies between the two group means.
# Near 1, the two groups differ a lot. Near 0, they have almost the same
# mean.
between <- sapply(X, function(v) {
  within <- sum(tapply(v, group, function(z) sum((z - mean(z))^2)))
  1 - within / sum((v - mean(v))^2)
})
round(sort(between, decreasing = TRUE), 3)

# Question: Name each group in two or three words. Which variables does
# your name rest on? Which variables barely differ between the two
# groups? Do not build a name on those.
```

```{r}
#| label: centers-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
# Why? The two centers from section 3 as a chart, variable by variable, in
# SDs. A bar to the right means the group is above the mean of all
# customers; a bar to the left means it is below.
centers_long <- data.frame(
  variable = factor(rep(colnames(km$centers), each = 2), levels = rev(vars)),
  group = factor(rep(1:2, times = ncol(km$centers))),
  z = as.vector(km$centers))
ggplot(centers_long, aes(x = variable, y = z, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("1" = "#1F5FA8", "2" = "#C41230")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Center (SDs from the mean of all customers)",
       fill = "Group", title = "The two centers, variable by variable") +
  theme_minimal()

# Question: On which variables do the two bars point in opposite
# directions? Among website, catalog and store purchases, which group
# buys more? Which group visits the website more?
```

```{r}
#| label: segment-plot
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
# Why? The clustering used 15 variables, and we cannot plot 15 axes.
# fviz_cluster() with choose.vars plots two of the file's own variables,
# in SDs, the units k-means worked in: income, the variable that differs
# most between the two groups, and meat spending, the spending variable
# that differs most. Each point is a customer, the large symbol is the
# group's center, and the ellipse covers the area where most of a group's
# points would fall if they spread like a normal distribution.
# ellipse.type = "convex" would plot the outline of each group instead.
# Student Note: without choose.vars, fviz_cluster() plots the groups on
# principal components (the PCA lab) instead of the variables in the file.
# The caption turns one SD back into dollars.
segment_plot <- fviz_cluster(list(data = Xs, cluster = group),
                             choose.vars = c("Income", "MntMeatProducts"),
                             geom = "point", ellipse.type = "norm",
                             palette = c("#1F5FA8", "#C41230"),
                             main = "Two segments on income and meat spending",
                             xlab = "Income (SDs from the mean)",
                             ylab = "Meat spending (SDs from the mean)",
                             ggtheme = theme_minimal())
segment_plot + labs(color = "Group", fill = "Group", shape = "Group") +
  labs(caption = paste0(
    "One SD of income is $", format(round(sd(X$Income)), big.mark = ","),
    ". One SD of meat spending is $", format(round(sd(X$MntMeatProducts)), big.mark = ","),
    ". K-means grouped customers in these standardized units."))

# Question: Where do the two groups overlap? Find a point of group 2 with
# a low income. What else could put that customer in group 2?
#
# Discuss: The picture shows 2 of the 15 variables. When a point sits
# among the other group's points, the other 13 variables are the reason.
# Do your names still describe most of the points of each color?
```

**Before you decide.** Talk with the person next to you. Look at the group
means, the centers chart and the picture. Write a short name for each
segment, the offer for its campaign, and the channel you would use to
reach it: the store, the website or the catalog.

```{r}
#| label: commit
# Type a name, an offer and a channel for each segment between the quotes.
name_1 <- ""
name_2 <- ""
offer_1 <- ""
offer_2 <- ""
channel_1 <- ""
channel_2 <- ""

if (all(nchar(c(name_1, name_2, offer_1, offer_2, channel_1, channel_2)) > 0)) {
  cat("Segment 1:", name_1, "|", km$size[1], "customers | Offer:", offer_1, "| Channel:", channel_1, "\n")
  cat("Segment 2:", name_2, "|", km$size[2], "customers | Offer:", offer_2, "| Channel:", channel_2, "\n")
} else {
  cat("Missing entries. Type a name, an offer and a channel for each segment",
      "between the quotes, then run this chunk again.\n")
}

# Business Insight: A good offer and channel use what the segment already
# does and how it differs from the other segment: where it visits and
# buys, what it buys, and how much it spends. Do not build them on
# variables that barely differ.
```

# 6. A second method: hierarchical clustering

**Why?** If a second method finds the same two groups, they are less
likely to be an accident of one method. Ward linkage, used below, works
with the same within-group sum of squares as k-means, so its groups are
easy to compare with k-means. Hierarchical clustering does not need k up
front. Each customer
starts as its own group. Then the two closest groups are joined, again
and again, until all customers are in one group. The dendrogram is a tree
diagram that records every join. With most linkages, the height of a join
is the distance between the two groups. With Ward linkage, used here, the
height is a merge cost: it grows with how much the join raises the
within-group sum of squares.

```{r}
#| label: hclust
# The linkage is the rule for choosing which two groups to join next:
#   "complete": the largest distance between a customer of one group and
#               a customer of the other
#   "average":  the average of all those distances
#   "ward.D2":  join the two groups that raise the within-group sum of
#               squares the least, the number k-means makes small
# The linkage is one setting: after class, change it here and run section
# 6 again to see another dendrogram. We reuse d, the distances from section 4.
# The Session 8 slides used "average" linkage. Here we use "ward.D2"
# because it aims at the same thing as k-means, so its two groups are
# easy to compare with section 3. After-class question 4 tries the others.
linkage <- "ward.D2"
hc <- hclust(d, method = linkage)
# Cut the dendrogram into two groups.
hc_group <- cutree(hc, k = 2)
table(hc_group)

# Question: How many customers are in each branch of the dendrogram?
```

```{r}
#| label: compare
# K-means down the side, hierarchical clustering across the top.
table(kmeans = group, hclust = hc_group)
# The mean of each variable in each branch.
round(sapply(split(X, hc_group), colMeans), 1)
# If one branch is very small, look at its customers one by one. With Ward
# both branches are large, so this prints nothing in class; it matters in
# after-class question 4.
small <- names(hc_group)[hc_group == names(which.min(table(hc_group)))]
if (length(small) <= 10) X[small, ]

# Question: Do k-means and hierarchical clustering find the same two
# groups? Hierarchical clustering numbers its branches its own way.
# Which branch goes with which k-means group, and how many customers
# do the two methods put in different groups? Which k-means group holds
# most of the customers they disagree on?
#
# Discuss: Which grouping would you take to the marketing team, and what
# would you tell them about the other one?
```

# 7. What can the grouping not tell the store?

**Before you write.** Look back at your names, offers and channels from section 5
and at what hierarchical clustering found in section 6. Write one limit
of this grouping. Then go back to the split you made at the start with
income and children only.

```{r}
#| label: limit
# Type one limit of this grouping between the quotes.
my_limit <- ""
if (nchar(my_limit) > 0) cat("Limit:", my_limit, "\n") else
  cat("No limit yet. Type one between the quotes, then run this chunk again.\n")

# One way to write the split from the start as a rule: customers with an
# income at or above the median and no small children at home (Kidhome is
# 0; teenagers do not count) go in group 2, everyone else in group 1.
simple <- ifelse(X$Income >= median(X$Income) & X$Kidhome == 0, 2, 1)
table(kmeans = group, simple = simple)
# The customers the rule puts in a different group from k-means: their
# means on six variables, by their k-means group.
moved <- simple != group
moved_means <- aggregate(X[moved, c("Income", "Kidhome", "Teenhome",
                                    "NumCatalogPurchases", "NumWebVisitsMonth",
                                    "MntMeatProducts")],
                         by = list(kmeans_group = group[moved]), FUN = mean)
moved_means[-1] <- round(moved_means[-1], 2)
moved_means

# Question: How many customers does the simple rule put in a different
# group from k-means? What kind of customer does it misplace?
#
# Discuss: Clustering uses no outcome variable. The file records whether
# each customer accepted six past campaigns. We left those flags out, and
# the file does not say what those offers were, which channel they used
# or what they cost. Nothing here says whether a customer bought more
# after an offer. What does the grouping not tell the store?
```

# 8. After class: extra questions

Work on these on your own after class. They use the same data and the
objects from sections 1 to 7.

1. **One start or twenty?** Run k-means with one start from 100 different
   seeds, at k = 2 and at k = 4. How many of the 100 runs reach the total
   within-group sum of squares of the 20-start run from section 4? How
   far off is the worst run?

2. **The original units, at more length.** Look at the groups from the
   run in the original units in section 2. What are their means? What
   share of the total sum of squares does income hold in the original
   units? Why does that decide the groups?

3. **The three early years of birth.** Drop the customers born in 1893,
   1899 and 1900, put the variables in SDs again, and rerun k-means with
   two groups. How many customers change group? Do your names change?

4. **The other linkages.** Cut the dendrogram at two groups with Ward
   (`"ward.D2"`), complete, average and single linkage. Which linkage
   agrees most with k-means? Which ones split off a small branch of a
   few customers, and who are they? To plot one of the dendrograms, set
   `linkage` in section 6 and run section 6 again.

5. **Three groups.** Run k-means with k = 3 and name the three groups from
   their means. Which of your two segments splits, and is the split one
   the store could use?

6. **Another picture of the segments.** Plot the two segments with
   `fviz_cluster()` on catalog purchases and website visits a month.
   Which channel would you use to reach each segment? Why do the points
   line up on a grid?

```{r}
#| label: after-class-starts
#| eval: false
# After class, change eval to true. Do not run these in class.
# One start from each of 100 seeds, at k = 2 and at k = 4.
one_start <- function(k) sapply(1:100, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  kmeans(Xs, centers = k, nstart = 1)$tot.withinss
})
wss_one2 <- one_start(2)
wss_one4 <- one_start(4)
# Runs out of 100 that reach the 20-start total from section 4, and the
# worst total, at k = 2 and k = 4.
c(k2 = sum(round(wss_one2, 1) == round(wss[["2"]], 1)),
  k4 = sum(round(wss_one4, 1) == round(wss[["4"]], 1)))
round(rbind(best_of_20 = wss[c("2", "4")], worst_one_start = c(max(wss_one2), max(wss_one4))), 1)
# The group sizes of the worst one-start run at k = 2.
set.seed(which.max(wss_one2))
kmeans(Xs, centers = 2, nstart = 1)$size
```

#| label: after-class-linkages

# The same distances, four linkages, each cut into two groups.
linkages <- c("ward.D2", "complete", "average", "single")
link_groups <- lapply(setNames(linkages, linkages), function(m)
  cutree(hclust(d, method = m), k = 2))
link_tab <- lapply(link_groups, function(g) table(kmeans = group, hclust = g))
link_tab
# Number of customers in the smaller branch for each linkage.
sapply(link_groups, function(g) sum(g == names(which.min(table(g)))))
# Who is in the small branch? Complete linkage is shown; average and single
# split off the same customers.
small_branch <- link_groups$complete ==
  names(which.min(table(link_groups$complete)))
X[small_branch, ]
